You do need to use steroid nasal sprays properly for them to work . " The biggest mistake people make is to ' sniff ' or ' snort ' their steroid nasal spray , which means it just ends up in the tummy and does n't help their symptoms at all , " Walker says . " You must let it sit inside your nose for a few hours in order for the anti-inflammatory effect to take hold and then the results are very good . " There is a useful video on using a steroid nasal spray correctly on asthmaandlung.org.uk . <h> Apply anti-inflammatory eyedrops four times a day <p> Itchy , inflamed or watery eyes are a big complaint for hay fever sufferers . The NHS says Vaseline works just as well . <h> Wash your hair and have a shower before bed <p> Biggs says that simple lifestyle strategies can " have a big impact on reducing symptoms " . Keep an eye on the Met Office daily pollen forecasts . " When pollen levels are high , shower and wash your hair when you get home to remove any traces , " she says . " This is especially important before bed to reduce the risk of pollen from your hair settling on your pillow . " Wear wraparound sunglasses to prevent pollen getting to your eyes , " Biggs says . <h> Drink a cup of matcha tea <p> Green tea may relieve allergic rhinitisGetty images <p> A new study @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of Food , suggests that the fashionable green tea powder could reduce the need to sneeze in people with hay fever . Matcha made from ground , shade-grown green tea leaves contains high levels of biologically active compounds including antioxidants . Mice given the tea two to three times a week for over five weeks , with a dose of tea 30 minutes before being exposed to an allergen , sneezed much less than expected . @@136590204 <h> The unusual ways Fijians predict when a cyclone is approaching <p> It 's July , a month when Fijian farmers begin watching wild yams closely . " If they see wild yam vines creeping along the ground , there 's going to be a hurricane in between November and April -- the hurricane season , " says farmer Marika Radua . If the vines shoot upwards , it 's unlikely a hurricane will hit , he says . <p> In the dense jungle on Vanua Levu , Fiji 's second largest island , Radua 's farm is a riot of green . Every plant has its place -- from rows of delicate lettuce , to sturdy taro and cassava . For years , Radua has read the signs in nature to know when , and where , to plant his crops to ensure they thrive each season . <p> Yam vines are natural indicators of extreme weather , according to Fijian traditional ecological knowledge . This environmental knowledge comprises ancient traditions held and practiced by indigenous peoples . When the vines hug the ground , " they are already @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nature , " Radua says . <p> Many Fijians -- especially those from older generations who are more likely to use traditional farming methods -- believe other organisms act as natural weather forecasts , such as bananas , bees and breadfruit . <p> Before modern technology , environmental indicators like these were used across the world to predict natural disasters . But in the last century , data from satellites , weather radars and computers has provided increasingly precise monitoring and forecasting . <p> In the Pacific , communities are returning to ancient wisdom to anticipate extreme weather , to enhance modern methods . Scientific studies and Fiji 's meteorological service are recording these local " early warning signs " of tropical cyclones and flooding . As climate-change-driven disasters pick up pace in the Pacific , traditional knowledge might buy communities more time to prepare . <h> A total package <p> In 2024 , the Fijian Meteorological Service announced it would integrate traditional environmental knowledge into its scientific forecasting -- describing the pair as " a total package " . <p> Fiji follows in the footsteps of Vanuatu , Tonga @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nations participating in an ongoing project to integrate traditional knowledge in their early-warning systems . <p> " In most parts of the world , traditional knowledge and national services are not mentioned in the same sentence , " says Lui . " But in the Pacific , it 's now becoming the go to . It 's normal practice . The app has a database of crowd-sourced natural indicators -- for example , green turtles nesting further inland suggests a cyclone may be approaching . <p> However , using traditional knowledge to preempt weather events is not an instant process , says Lui . <p> " You can not integrate a data set that 's only five years old with a data set that 's 100 years old . The economic benefit argument is boosted further because any taxes received will be turbocharged ; firstly by the extremely high gas price , which boosts company profits without them doing anything . And , secondly , by an additional windfall tax of 25 per cent on oil and gas company profits that was introduced in 2022 ( and which has raised about ? 12bn from North Sea production so far ) . <p> Much of that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , offer more grants for solar panels and heat pumps -- and potentially to subsidise new wind and solar farms , so that households foot less of the bill . <p> And the amounts of money to be made from North Sea taxes are significant . And gas-fired power plants are still used to generate 30 per cent of the country 's electricity , with low-carbon sources such as solar and wind providing much of the rest -- along with nuclear ( although repeated experience tells us that this always takes much longer to build , and at a much higher cost , than original estimates ) . <p> Even under the fastest decarbonisation scenario , the UK would continue to need a fair bit of electricity as it transitions to a green energy system . @@136601603 <h> Breadcrumb <h> The legal block on climate action <p> Colombia has sent a strong signal about corporate influence over its climate policies as it gears up to host the first Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels . Can the world follow ? <p> No government should have to choose between protecting nature and its people , and protecting itself from arbitrators . <p> Colombia is to withdraw from the Investor-State Dispute Settlement ( ISDS ) , an opaque mechanism allowing foreign investors to sue governments for decisions that affect their profits , including those aimed at protecting human rights , worker rights , health and the environment . <p> Cases are heard by international arbitration tribunals rather than national courts . There are no independent judges , nor a right to appeal . The tribunals are closed to citizens , companies , NGOs and the media . <p> The grounds for the case are not published , nor are decisions . Compensation paid by governments to corporations comes from public budgets . <p> The mechanism has frequently been used by fossil fuel companies to block or deter climate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ launched more ISDS cases than any other sector . <p> In fact , disputes in the oil , gas and mining sectors accounted for the largest portion of new claims filed in 2025 , representing 45 per cent of new cases , the ICSID found . This is a sharp increase from 25 per cent in the previous year and compares to a 26 per cent historical average . <p> Transition <p> They also tend to win . In total , fossil fuel businesses have reaped at least US$100 billion , Boyd 's report found . The average award in published arbitration awards concerning fossil fuels is $600 million -- five times the average amount awarded in arbitrations related to non-fossil fuels . <p> Large awards are made even if corporations have made next to no investment , because companies can sue for the amount that they calculate that they would have extracted for the length of the term of the concession . <p> No government should have to choose between protecting nature and its people , and protecting itself from arbitrators . <p> Critics of ISDS say that it @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ blocks climate action both directly through forcing governments to divert funding they could spend on the transition , and indirectly through putting them off regulations that could land them in front of tribunals . <p> Governments including New Zealand and Denmark have admitted to delaying restrictions on fossil fuel projects for fear of attracting ISDS arbitration . The Spanish government has also commented on how ISDS was being used to prevent energy transition after more than 50 ISDS claims , seeking compensation totalling more than $11 billion , were filed against it . <p> The Colombian government currently has 28 ISDS cases filed against it , 16 of which are concerned with fossil fuel extraction , according to Louise Winstanley , programme and advocacy manager for campaign organisation AB Colombia . <p> These include mining giant Glencore suing the Colombian government for $489 million after the country 's Constitutional Court suspended a proposed expansion to the Cerrej ? n open-pit coal mine in 2017 due to its impacts on the environment , health and human and indigenous rights . <p> The total value of the claims against Colombia is estimated @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The risk of having to pay out substantial amounts of money is blocking Colombia 's ability to restrict fossil fuels . " <p> " This dynamic raises significant concerns about states ' ability to regulate freely in the public interest , including in the context of climate action , " they added . <p> Observers welcomed the move , saying it sent an important signal ahead of the Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels it is hosting in Santa Marta at the end of April . <p> Discriminated <p> Though the announcement was a reiteration of a previous pledge made by Petro , campaigners hope that action will be rapid . An election for the presidency is slated for 31 May , notes Tom Wills @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ If anything is going to happen , it 's going to have to happen really fast , and with the support of Colombia 's investment treaty partners , including the UK , " he says . <p> A spokesperson for the Foreign , Commonwealth and Development Office said : " Our Bilateral Investment Treaty with Colombia helps both UK and Colombian investors resolve disputes where they claim to have been unfairly treated or discriminated against without compensation . <p> " We continue to work with trading partners , including the OECD and the UN to improve the system , " they added . <p> Withdrawal <p> The number of known ISDS cases targeting actions taken by states to protect the environment has skyrocketed , from 12 initiated prior to 2000 to 37 in the period 2000 -- 2010 and 126 in the period 2011 -- 2021 , Boyd 's report revealed . <p> Last year saw 63 new cases lodged , the second highest in the mechanism 's history after 2021 , when 66 cases were initiated , according to data from the International Centre for Settlement of Investor Disputes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> However , in recent years , several countries have pulled out of ISDS due to its incompatibility with climate change action . <p> Even countries in the Global North , including traditionally strong supporters of ISDS , are shifting , he says , pointing to Australia , which no longer includes ISDS in new treaties and has sought to remove such provisions from existing ones , and the US and Canada which have eliminated ISDS in their renegotiated North American trade agreement . <p> Since then , EU states including Germany , France , Spain and the Netherlands have exited the ECT , though others adopted a modernised version . @@136602980 <p> A study led by researchers at the University of Cambridge and collaborators in Vancouver have uncovered how age-related changes in breast tissue may increase cancer risk . By sequencing individual cells , the team constructed a detailed map of breast tissue comprising over three million cells . They also used a technique known as imaging mass cytometry ( IMC ) to map the spatial organisation of these cells within the tissue . <p> The study found that cell numbers of all types declined steadily with age , with the most pronounced losses occurring during and after menopause . Key structures in the tissue shrink , leaving the tissue less resilient and more vulnerable to DNA damage . <p> " Cell numbers of all types declined steadily with age , with the most pronounced losses during menopause " <p> This reduction in cellular diversity , combined with hormonal changes , appears to create conditions that favour cancer development -- helping to explain why four out of five breast cancer cases occur in women over 50 . The findings could improve risk prediction and inform new strategies for early detection and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ will there be a super El Ni ? o ? <p> Researchers at the European Centre For Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ( ECMWF ) are warning that this year 's El Ni ? o event could be among the strongest ever reported . If so , it may drastically reshape weather patterns worldwide . <p> El Ni ? o is part of a natural Pacific Ocean cycle that oscillates between La Ni ? a and El Ni ? o phases . During La Ni ? a , the wind pushes warm water westward , allowing cooler water to rise in the eastern Pacific . This temporarily suppresses global temperatures , masking the warming effects of human-driven climate change . During El Ni ? o , however , the wind weakens and reverses : warm water accumulates in the eastern Pacific , raising global temperatures and disrupting weather systems . Depending on the region , El Ni ? o can increase flood risk , intensify droughts , and shift hurricane activity . <p> Researchers are already reporting rising ocean temperatures -- an early sign that the system is transitioning into an El @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ wind patterns and sea surface temperatures to determine whether a devastating ' super El Ni ? o ' ( defined by a temperature increase exceeding 2 ? C ) will develop . In regions susceptible to drought and flooding , early preventative measures are already being encouraged . <p> However , forecasting remains uncertain due to the so-called ' spring prediction barrier ' , which limits accuracy . In 2014 , for instance , a major El Ni ? o was forecast but ultimately failed to materialise . By June , however , predictions should become more reliable . With geopolitical tensions and supply chain pressures already straining global systems , a strong El Ni ? o could further drive up food prices and inflation . <h> Dwarfs , digital cameras , and discovery : uncovering the history of our galaxy <p> The Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile is set to transform astronomy with its decade-long Legacy Survey of Space and Time ( LSST ) , which will soon take the longest continuous image of the universe . Using early LSST data , astronomers have already identified 17 new @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ once the survey is fully underway , more than 17,000 such objects could be discovered . <p> Brown dwarfs are dying remains of failed stars -- too small to sustain hydrogen fusion -- and emit light primarily in the infrared , making them invisible to the naked eye . However , LSST 's infrared-sensitive filters allow astronomers to detect this faint emission and distinguish these objects from background noise . <p> Despite their dimness , brown dwarfs are scientifically valuable because they preserve the chemical signatures of the gas clouds from which they formed ; they offer insight into the early chemistry of the Milky Way . Their atmospheres also resemble those of exoplanets , making them useful analogues for understanding exoplanet behaviour . <p> As LSST begins its full survey , astronomers are preparing for a wave of discoveries . @@136606886 <h> Giant lake suddenly returns 130 years after vanishing <p> The once huge Lake Tululare fully disappeared in around 1890 but then returned in 2023 <p> ( Mario Tama/Getty Images ) <p> Tulare Lake , located in California 's San Joaquin Valley , was once one of the largest bodies of freshwater in the whole of the US . <p> But , some 130 years ago it disappeared -- thanks largely to the greed of colonialists , who drained its waters to create arable farmland . <p> And yet , last year , the once-cherished lake suddenly reemerged , bringing with it both positive and painful effects . <p> Back in the late 19th Century , Tulare stretched more than 100 miles long and 30 miles wide , and was " the largest body of freshwater west of the Mississippi River " , Vivian Underhill of Northeastern University explained in a news release . <p> At this time , it contained so much water that a steamship could carry " agricultural supplies from the Bakersfield area up to Fresno ( at the heart of the San Joaquin Valley ) and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ nearly 300 miles -- she said . <p> However , in the succeeding decades , the " ancestral lakes " and connecting waterways that made such a route possible all but vanished thanks to manmade irrigation . <p> Named " Pa'ashi " by the indigenous Tachi Yokut tribe , Tulare Lake was fed primarily by snowmelt out of the Sierra Nevada mountains , as opposed to rainfall , which is scant in the region . <p> Fresno receives just over 10 inches of rain a year on average and sometimes as little as three , according to the National Weather Service . <p> Looking at the arid landscape of the San Joaquin Valley over the course of the 21st Century , it would have been hard to imagine such a large body of water dominating the landscape . <p> However , in the 1800s , " Fresno was a lakeside town , " Underhill said . <p> Fresno , at the heart of the San Joaquin Valley , is an arid place that receives little rainfall ( PATRICK T. FALLON/AFP via Getty Images ) <p> The researcher , who specialises @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first began disappearing in the late 1850s and early 1860s , thanks to " the state of California 's desire to take historically indigenous land and put it into private ownership . " <p> This process was called " reclamation " and often entailed " either draining inundated land or irrigating desert land to create arable farmland " , she said . <p> If " people could drain that land , " they would " be granted ownership of parts of that land . So there was a big incentive for white settlers to start doing that work , " she added , describing the process as a " deeply settler colonial project " . <p> The first time the lake fully disappeared was around 1890 , when its " water essentially was used to irrigate all of the arid lands around that area , " she went on . <p> " Now the valley is crisscrossed by hundreds of irrigation canals , all of which were originally built to take that lake water and put it onto irrigated fields . " <p> And yet , in 2023 , Tulare @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ great river was reborn last year ( Mario Tama/Getty Images ) <p> " California just got inundated with snow in the winter and then rain in the spring , " Underhill explained . <p> " If you have a rain and snow event , the snow melts really fast , " and all of this still runs into the depression where Tulare Lake once sat . <p> Months after the lake 's resurgence , the impacts could be seen in the local wildlife . <p> " Birds of all kinds -- pelicans , hawks , waterbirds " are returning , Underhill said , adding that " the Tachi also say that they 've seen burrowing owls nesting around the shore , " a species described as " vulnerable or imperilled " by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service . <p> As well as the homecoming of different species -- including fish and amphibians likely brought down by rainfall and flooding -- human communities have been greatly affected by the lake 's rebirth . <p> For the Tachi Yokuts , " the return of the lake has been just an incredibly @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ " They 've been holding ceremonies on the side of the lake . They 've been able to practice their traditional hunting and fishing practices again . " <p> The lake has brought with it the return of numerous species , including wetland birds ( Mario Tama/Getty Images ) <p> However , for the region 's farmworkers and landowners , the picture has been far less rosy . <p> Many of these agricultural workers have suffered devastating losses as a result of the flooding , with many losing their homes entirely . <p> Efforts are already underway to drain the lake once again , and Underhill said she expects it to remain in some form for about two more years -- although new atmospheric river events over California this year could complicate this . <p> " Under climate change , " Underhill says , " floods of this magnitude or higher will happen with increasing frequency . " <p> " At a certain point , I think it would behove the state of California to realize that Tulare Lake wants to remain . And in fact , there 's a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it remain . " <p> She also noted that last year 's resurrection was n't the lake 's first return since the 1800s . <p> " It happened in the ' 80s , it happened once in the ' 60s , a couple of times in the ' 30s , " she said . <p> Looking at the wider environmental context , Underhill pointed out : " This landscape has always been one of lakes and wetlands , and our current irrigated agriculture is just a century-long blip in this larger geologic history . " <p> " This was not actually a flood . This is a lake returning . " <p> More than 100 square miles of farms and other land were flooded last year ( Mario Tama/Getty Images ) <p> Nevertheless , in March this year , a reporter for the Guardian went to visit the iconic lake , and found herself met with " sprouts of grass and thick mud " . <p> Less than a year after its revival , Tulare Lake had shrunk to just 2,625 acres , according to the Kings county office of emergency services .

But that 's not to say nature has n't changed here -- sometimes for the worse . <p> Timothy Mousseau/ CFF <p> Feral dogs -- descendants of pets abandoned around Chernobyl -- now roam close to the containment shield where the devastated reactor is now housed ( Credit : Timothy Mousseau/ CFF ) <h> Genetic mutations <p> Burraco and his colleagues have visited Chernobyl and the surrounding areas many times over the years , sampling more than 250 tree frogs in total . In 2022 , they published data indicating that frogs inside the exclusion zone were , on average , darker than those outside the zone . They focused on locations where radiation levels were particularly high immediately after the accident in 1986 . <p> Their hypothesis , which Burraco emphasises remains a hypothesis , is that the dark colour of some frogs -- attributed to higher levels of melanin in their bodies -- might somehow act as a protective barrier , reducing the effects of radiation , and that darker frogs fared better in the aftermath of the nuclear disaster @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> Germa'n Orizaola <p> Some frogs in the Chernobyl contamination zone have darker skin , which has been proposed as an adaptation to the radiation in the environment ( Credit : Germa'n Orizaola ) <p> One researcher , biologist Timothy Mousseau at the University of South Carolina , is critical of the tree frogs study . He says the sampling of frogs was not comprehensive enough to show a distinction between those inside and outside the exclusion zone , arguing that the occurrence of melanisation does not correlate with current levels of radioactivity around the Chernobyl disaster site . <p> Burraco pushes back against these points . The frogs , he notes , were sampled from a variety of areas with differing radiological exposures that are otherwise similar in terms of habitat , for example . He also notes that radiation levels have changed since the time of the accident . <p> Another scientist , radiobiologist Carmel Mothersill , professor emeritus at McMaster University , says the 2022 paper is " sound " in terms of its methodology and she points out that the authors are cautious in how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a classic example of the kind of disagreement that has bubbled away for years among scientific investigators of Chernobyl 's wildlife . First there is the question of responses -- how do you know that some unusual feature documented in an organism is caused specifically by exposure to radiation and not , say , other contaminants in the landscape such as heavy metals , which are also known to pollute the area ? <p> Similar debates surround reports about genetic patterns in the genomes of feral dogs living around Chernobyl , for example . There 's no hard evidence that this was caused by their exposure to radiation . Studies have also shown that bank voles living in contaminated sites around Chernobyl carry higher levels of genetic diversity in their mitochondria -- the tiny energy generators inside their cells -- compared to those in non-contaminated areas . These differences might be attributable to mutations caused by exposure to radiation but other factors could also be at work . <h> A changed landscape <p> Mothersill points out that many pine trees , which are especially sensitive to radiation , died @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ some locations , she says , creating a completely different kind of forest : " It 's teeming with trees and wildlife but it 's not the same as it was before the accident . " Animals living there will naturally respond differently to that changed environment and this alone , rather than radiation per se , could explain differences in those animals . <p> Getty Images <p> After residents were evacuated following the Chernobyl disaster , the forest began to take over the town of Pripyat in modern-day Ukraine ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> In areas once frequented by people , wolves , bears and bison now roam . Populations of deer , wild boar and elk have flourished . The number of wolves has even been estimated to be seven times higher in the exclusion zone compared to surrounding nature reserves , perhaps thanks to the abundant prey . Species including the Eurasian lynx have also returned to the area after vanishing long before the accident . <h> Adapting to survive ? <p> Leaving the other factors aside , is it possible that plants and animals @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ This is one of the most controversial claims of all . Some of the unusual characteristics of these organisms could be described as true adaptations in the evolutionary sense -- that is , things they have inherited and give them an edge in their environment . <p> Mousseau says that the black fungus growing within the stricken reactor building , where radiation levels remain very high , seems to be benefitting from that darker colour . " That 's significant , that 's positive evidence supporting the hypothesis that melanin provides some level of resistance to the effects of ionising radiation , " he says . <p> There 's still no answer to the question about whether darker frogs evolved their colour as an adaptation to protect them from radiation . <p> For Mothersill , it 's important to tease out whether mutations that emerged in plants and animals immediately after the accident have been passed down to successive generations of those organisms , even while radiation levels have fallen in the environment over time . Transgenerational mutations , if you like . <p> There is a hint of this @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that aberrations in the animals ' chromosomes persisted over successive generations even when voles were taken away from Chernobyl and allowed to reproduce in a contamination-free laboratory . <p> Getty Images <p> Elk have been documented in growing numbers following the evacuation of humans from the exclusion zone around Chernobyl ( Credit : Getty Images ) <p> Certainly , not all species are thriving . Recent research has found that the combination of heat emitted from radioactive contamination and rising temperatures from climate change are together placing growing strain on barn swallows living around Chernobyl , which may make it harder for them to survive as global warming continues . <p> The story of how Chernobyl has affected wildlife is complicated , argues Jonathon Turnbull , a geographer at Durham University . You ca n't just say nature in the exclusion zone is thriving or dying , he says : " There 's the spectacular story of ' Chernobyl changed everything ' -- that does n't go very deep . " <p> Rather , there exists a menagerie of subtle effects and responses . An entire ecosystem that experienced a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ no surprise , says Turnbull , that so many questions still litter this landscape 40 years on .

@@136657405 <p> Britain might be hit by record temperatures this summer as the world braces for a ' super El Ni ? o ' , according to experts . The weather phenomenon is characterised by sustained warm temperatures across the Pacific Ocean and is part of a natural cycle known as the El Ni ? o -- Southern Oscillation . It can impact places across the globe , including drier conditions in Australia to wetter weather in California . Meteorologists say El Ni ? o 's intensity will likely be comparable to the 1997/98 event , which saw global temperatures reach their highest on record . @@136657991 <h> World-leading expert on the impact of winds on high structures such as Canary Wharf and a prolific author of meteorological academic treatises <h> Share this article <p> In 1965 , gale-force winds toppled three of the eight huge cooling towers at the Ferrybridge power station in Yorkshire . Julian Hunt was a lanky PhD student at Cambridge at the time , and the incident piqued his interest . <p> A few years later , he identified the cause . The high winds had formed frequent eddies behind the close-packed cylindrical towers that " resonated " with the structures until they collapsed . From that deduction , he went on to expand and develop the " rapid distortion theory " , which applies whenever turbulent winds meet large obstructions . <p> Over the subsequent decades , Hunt became one of the world 's leading experts on winds -- or more specifically , their impact on buildings and other high structures , their role in trapping or dispersing air pollution , and their behaviour in hilly terrains . <p> Hunt with his son , Tristram , who became a Labour MP @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a prolific author of academic treatises . His research in the field of fluid dynamics had many practical applications . They included the engineering of structures ranging from North Sea oil rigs to skyscraper clusters such as Canary Wharf in London ; the design of cities and urban landscapes around the world ; the measuring of polluting emissions from traffic and tall chimney stacks ; and the precise shape of Airbus aircraft wings . <p> Hunt also brought his interest in air flows and ocean currents to bear on the problem of climate change . He used his five years as head of the UK 's Meteorological Office in the 1990s to draw attention to the increasingly apparent consequences , and to foster international co-operation in the battle to mitigate them . <p> Advertisement <p> Julian Charles Roland Hunt was born in Ootacamund , a hill station in the southern Indian state of Tamil Nadu , in 1941 . He was the first of five children of Roland Hunt , a Madras-based magistrate and tax collector in the Indian civil service , and his wife , Pauline , daughter of @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Nations . <p> The family returned to the UK at the end of the Second World War and settled in Oxford , where Hunt attended the private Dragon School before boarding at Westminster . <p> He saw little of his parents while growing up because his father joined the diplomatic service , later serving as deputy high commissioner in Pakistan and Uganda and high commissioner in Trinidad and Tobago when Hunt was an adult . <p> Hunt spent the school holidays with assorted great aunts . One , Dorothy , was married to Lewis Fry Richardson , a leading mathematician who ran the Meteorological Office 's Eskdalemuir observatory in southern Scotland . Richardson pioneered mathematical techniques for weather forecasting and had a big influence on his young guest . <p> Hunt won a place at Trinity College , Cambridge , to study mechanical sciences . A brilliant student , he was awarded a scholarship after his second year exams and graduated with a first-class honours degree in 1963 . <p> Advertisement <p> By then he had met Marylla Shephard , a landscape architect , at a tea party in Putney @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Jemima , now a journalist , novelist and Labour councillor in Oxford ; Matilda , a doctor in Norwich ; and Tristram , a former Labour MP who is now director of the Victoria and Albert Museum . <p> Hunt on his wedding day to Marylla Shephard in 1965 <p> Hunt first developed an interest in fluid dynamics during his final year as an undergraduate when he studied the impact of waves on beaches . The Met Office , as it is now known , was in the process of becoming a semi-privatised trading fund , and Hunt 's most pressing task was to ensure it could earn its keep by selling its weather forecasting and other services to institutions such as the BBC . <p> He used the post to encourage the sharing of climate data with other meteorological services around the world , acting as Britain 's permanent representative at the World Meteorological Organisation ( WMO ) . @@136671906 <p> Energy is messy , political and impossible to reduce to a single answer . Ian Ord has built Fifth Ring by embracing that complexity , not simplifying it . This is a story about expertise , authority and why the future lies in the mix , not the fix . <p> The best agency leaders know their clients ' businesses and markets just as well as ( and often better than ) the clients do . Ian Ord embodies that . He has built Fifth Ring by understanding not just marketing , but the energy industry itself , its pressures , its politics and its future . <p> I have known Ian Ord for more than 40 years . <p> We both started our careers in Aberdeen , our hometown , when the city was roaring with North Sea confidence and the energy industry was shaping not just the local economy but a whole generation of business careers . Ian was a young media sales executive at the Evening Express and The Press &amp; Journal . I was a fledgling agency executive . Neither of us could have known @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ also give Ian the foundations for building one of the world 's most respected specialist B2B agencies . <p> Today , Ord is the owner and director of business development of Fifth Ring , the Aberdeen-founded business he has turned into a global marketing specialist with energy at its heart . I wanted to interview him for my Agency Leaders series because this is a critical moment for the energy sector . The current geopolitical turmoil , the renewed instability in global fuel markets and the long shadow of climate change have combined to make energy one of the defining business and political stories of our time . <p> Ord is an agency leader , certainly . But he is also much more than that . He is one of those rare marketers who has become a genuine authority in the industry he serves . Speak to him for five minutes and it becomes obvious that his value to clients goes far beyond campaigns , brand platforms or lead generation . He understands the forces shaping their markets , the economics driving their decisions and the long-term tensions between affordability @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is not accidental . It is the product of decades spent building a business around a clear belief : that the best agencies do not try to be all things to all clients . <p> " When you start an agency , " Ord tells me , " you think all business is welcome . Consumer , B2B , any discipline , anything at all . It 's that classic entrepreneurial instinct that everything is good and everything is possible . But over time , as many businesses discover , if you can find the niche , if you can define your operating space , then you begin to prosper . You create that lighthouse identity that people gravitate towards . " <p> That realization shaped Fifth Ring 's future . Founded in 1991 with Clif Collier , the now CEO of the respected BBN B2B agency network , the agency did not begin as a specialist business . Like many ambitious independent agencies of that era , it took on a broad spread of work . But about 10 years in , Ord and his team made a strategic @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the familiar expansion path into Edinburgh , Glasgow or London , they chose internationalization and specialism . <p> Advertisement <p> " For some reason , there is always this gravitational pull to London , or to the nearest big city , " he says , " because the streets are supposed to be paved with gold . But if you arrive there and compete on level terms , you are only ever competing on level terms , or worse , because others are already there with established networks , communities and reputations . " <p> Fifth Ring chose a different route . It looked at where it had real credibility and asked itself what it genuinely knew better than most . The answer was energy . Back then , that largely meant oil and gas . Aberdeen gave the agency proximity to the industry , relationships within it and a working understanding of the commercial ecosystem around it . <p> That became the basis of a global strategy . <p> Ord says : " We asked ourselves what we could credibly claim to be good at . We knew a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ if we designed a business that better served our clients rather than necessarily served ourselves , would that not be attractive to them ? Would that not , by default , grow the business ? " <p> It did . The first big step came in the Middle East after a major client moved its marketing and business development function to Sharjah . Fifth Ring could have serviced the account remotely , embedded someone into the client team or sought a local partner . Instead , it established its own regional presence . Dubai followed in 2004 , then Houston in 2008 and Singapore in 2012 . <p> That strategy was not about planting flags for the sake of it . It was rooted in client need and sector logic . <p> " If we established businesses where our clients had a market , then we would differentiate ourselves by default , " Ord says . " We would be better placed , better shaped and better immersed in the vertical . That would make us harder to dislodge . " <p> That immersion has made Fifth Ring more than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it part of the energy conversation itself . And this is a fascinating time to be having that conversation . <h> Want to go deeper ? Ask The Drum <p> For all the noise around net zero , ESG and the transition to greener forms of power , Ord believes the industry is once again being shaped most powerfully by two hard-edged realities : security of supply and affordability . <p> " It 's such an important question , " he says when I ask him how the sector has changed in recent years . " If you go back four or five years , there was a huge drive towards ESG reporting . Every client in the energy space and beyond was hyper-conscious of carbon footprint , environmental responsibility and all the rest of it . But it bred a lot of vanilla messaging . Everybody had a solution . Everybody had an environmental responsibility story . You could play buzzword bingo with the positioning . " <p> Now , he argues , the mood has shifted . " What has become really interesting is that security of supply @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's not to say people have abandoned the need to be environmentally responsible . They have n't . But in the commercial world , the cost of becoming environmentally friendly can be prohibitive and people default to affordability . " <p> That is a crucial point and one that has profound implications not just for energy companies but for the marketers who serve them . The dominant story in energy is no longer a simple morality tale of old versus new , oil versus wind , dirty versus clean . It is more complicated than that . It is about resilience , economics , infrastructure and the political consequences of price shocks . <p> Ord puts it bluntly : " The energy industry is probably the biggest industry in the world . It is certainly one of the most consequential . If energy prices rise , then transport prices rise , food prices rise , fertilizer prices rise , everything rises . It has a direct effect on people 's lives and on governments ' ability to govern . " <p> That helps explain why he sees the current crisis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> " The unfortunate consequence is nationalism with a small ' n ' . Countries become much more self-focused in terms of their own energy supply . Politicians know they are not going to get elected if there are blackouts or if fuel becomes unaffordable . So the frame becomes , ' How do we secure our own energy , how do we make it affordable and how do we reduce exposure to shocks elsewhere ? ' " <p> That , in turn , is changing the kinds of opportunities Fifth Ring is seeing . While the agency remains best known for its deep roots in oil and gas , Ord has spent the last several years broadening both the firm 's definition of energy and its portfolio of sector expertise . The business has diversified into adjacent B2B sectors , including maritime , tech and manufacturing , while also moving with the changing shape of the energy market itself . <p> One of the most interesting areas right now , he says , is off-grid technology . " So many businesses have got to a point of either @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ where they need to establish their own power supply . They need to go off-grid . That is being driven by the growth in data centers , by the weakness of parts of the US grid and by the simple need for resilience . " <p> Advertisement <p> This , perhaps , is where Ord is most impressive . He does not talk like a man recycling agency jargon around a fashionable category . He talks like someone who has spent years listening to clients , studying the market and understanding the practical realities behind the briefing document . <p> He is also refreshingly skeptical about miracle cures . " Everybody you talk to believes they 've got a silver bullet . I do n't believe that 's the case . I think the answer lies in the hands of the individual or business that can integrate a system to make it work . It 's not one component or one source of fuel that changes the outcome . It 's about looking at the need and asking , ' Can I harness wind , can I harness solar , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ heat I can convert , what does peak demand look like ? ' It is the integration that matters . " <p> Which leads him to a phrase I suspect many in the sector would do well to remember . " It 's not about the energy fix . It 's about the energy mix . " <p> That mix , in Ord 's view , will continue to include oil and gas , not simply because transport still depends on them but because the wider modern economy does too . <p> " People often think of oil and gas only as petrol or diesel . But it is roads , plastics , all the materials and products that make modern life what it is . There will always be an oil and gas business . The question is how it evolves , how it coexists with other sources and how businesses and countries become more resilient in the way they consume energy . " <p> He is equally clear that nuclear must remain part of the conversation , despite its political baggage . <p> " Nuclear is probably one @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most abundant and one of the cheapest to generate once established . The problem is the cost of construction and the legacy of what happens when things go wrong . That has given it a bad reputation . But it is very definitely part of the mix and it is interesting that something once treated almost as a pariah is now being reconsidered in a much more serious way . " <p> If this sounds more like the analysis of an industry strategist than the words of an agency leader , that is precisely the point . <p> Advertisement <p> The best specialist agencies are built on this kind of authority . Clients do not simply want communications suppliers . They want partners who understand the forces acting upon their business , can help them navigate change and can frame their story in a way that is both credible and commercially intelligent . That is what Fifth Ring has built its reputation on . <p> Ord 's journey also says something important about the value of staying rooted in where you come from . Aberdeen , for all its changes @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the world and a point of view on it that no amount of superficial category hopping could ever replicate . He built from there , internationally and intelligently , rather than following a more conventional agency growth script . <p> And yet there is another side to him , too . Throughout our conversation , what also comes through is a strong sense of civic responsibility and public service . Ord now serves as deputy lord lieutenant of the city of Aberdeen , helping strengthen ties between the city and the crown and , more importantly , helping recognize the people and organizations doing meaningful work in the community . <p> He speaks particularly warmly about supporting recognition for local initiatives such as the Russell Anderson Foundation , which has done extraordinary work to widen access to sport , nutrition and opportunity for young people across Aberdeen . <p> It is easy to dismiss such things as the nice add-on chapter in a business leader 's life . In Ord 's case , they feel more integral than that . They reflect a seriousness about contribution , place and stewardship @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> That may be why our conversation , although ostensibly about energy , keeps circling back to responsibility . Responsibility to clients . Responsibility to markets . Responsibility to communities . Responsibility , even , to the truth of a category , rather than simply the fashionable version of it . <p> Agency leaders like Ian Ord are rare . Plenty can talk a good game about sector expertise . Much fewer have built an enduring business on it . Fewer still can range from the history of oil and gas to the politics of nuclear , from the economics of off-grid power to the practical realities of client transformation -- and do so with the calm authority of someone who has spent decades in the engine room . <p> More than 40 years on from those early Aberdeen days , Ord has become exactly the kind of leader modern B2B marketing needs : commercially sharp , strategically grounded and deeply fluent in the world his clients operate in . @@136674239 <p> What do racism , climate change , immigration and fuel costs all have in common ? They have all sparked protests in Ireland over the past five years . Ireland is once again in a rush to catch up with our fellow western nations , such that protest is increasingly the primary language of our politics , both for the Left and the Right . No one seems happy with the status quo , each protest being an expression of the division , disunity and anger that increasingly characterises the political scene in the West . Despite the efforts of politicians and policy experts to come to grips with why this is the case , one of the few world leaders who truly has an answer is our own Pope Leo XIV . <p> In a post on X/Twitter on April 18 , Pope Leo outlined @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ' Faith does not separate the spiritual from the social . ' <p> Leo 's comments are a good summary of the weakness of our present status quo : liberalism , with its claim to neutrality between different conceptions of the good towards which man is directed . But as liberalism has no unifying vision , our local institutions and structures can be no more than a locus of conflict and self-interest , different groups vying for a certain bottom line of economic prosperity and political power . @@136675523 <h> The Clwyd constituency straddles parts of the North Wales counties of Conwy , Denbighshire , Flintshire and Wrexham <p> Residents across the Westminster constituencies of Clwyd East and Clwyd North will be united under a single , expansive new constituency simply known as Clwyd at this election . Six Senedd Members will be returned from the area . <p> The boundary alterations are a direct consequence of sweeping reforms to devolved elections across Wales . Alongside the constituency changes , both the voting system and the number of elected representatives are set to change significantly . <p> For the election on May 7 , sixteen constituencies will each return six Senedd Members . Rather than the existing 60 Senedd members , the chamber will expand to 96 , while the voting system will also be overhauled . Voters will no longer cast two separate ballots for a constituency and regional member , but instead cast a single vote for a party . Please find a guide to all the changes here . <h> Constituency map <h> The candidates <p> Like all 16 of the new super-constituencies for Senedd elections @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ election . <p> ? <p> People will vote for a party and the successful candidates will be chosen by a system of proportional representation using the votes in the constituency . If a party was to win all the votes in an area , it would be allocated all six seats . However it 's more likely that the seats will be split between several parties . <p> Political parties have published lists of up to eight candidates for each constituency and if a party wins one seat in a constituency , the name at the top of their list will be elected . If a party wins two seats in a constituency , the top two names on their list will be elected , and so on . Independent candidates can also stand . <p> We have asked all parties to provide a list of all their candidates , and biographies of their top four candidates . " <p> Dr Whale explained that cloud seeding does exist but is a separate and limited form of weather modification , but does not create rain or clouds from blue sky . <p> It involves dispersing substances into clouds to induce rainfall or reduce hail , and is not used to create clouds from clear skies . <p> Whale explained that current conditions in the sky mean that the trails stick around for much longer , and long they last depends on the temperature and humidity of the air the plane if flying through . <p> He said : " Meteorological conditions will have favoured persistent contrails that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ has gone , and spreading out , meaning you can see lots of them at one time . <p> " You can see that they have varying degrees of sharpness -- the fresh ones are much narrower . <p> According to a Freedom of Information ( FOI ) request in 2013 , the Department of Energy and Climate Change confirmed the UK Government did fund cloud seeding experiments in the 1950s - but there is little evidence to suggest since then that the UK carries out this practice . <p> A similar FOI request to the UK Health Security Agency found the agency did not hold any information about cloud seeding as " we are not overseeing the UK cloud seeding operation " , signposting to the Department of Environment , Food and Rural Affairs ' pollution tracker . <h> Useful Links <p> This website and associated newspapers adhere to the Independent Press Standards Organisation 's Editors ' Code of Practice . @@136725381 <h> Top geopolitical risks that will shape African economies <p> Over the past decades , the global order has undergone significant transformation . Many analysts argue that the post-Cold War unipolar system , led by the United States , is gradually evolving into a more fragmented and multipolar landscape . Global dynamics are increasingly shaped by competing interests between advanced and emerging economies , democratic and authoritarian systems , as well as broader divisions between the Global North and Global South . At the same time , rivalry among major powers and the growing influence of middle powers are adding further complexity to the international system . <p> Against this backdrop , African economies -- many of which are still in early stages of industrial and economic transformation -- are likely to face a more uncertain and challenging external environment . Rapid population growth , combined with structural economic constraints and climate-related pressures , adds further strain . Together , these dynamics are expected to amplify a range of geopolitical and economic risks across the continent . <h> Fragmentation of the Rules-Based International Order <p> The rules-based international order has @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trade , finance , and diplomacy . This system has facilitated economic integration and supported growth in many parts of the world , including several African economies . <p> However , in recent years , there has been growing concern about increasing fragmentation within this system . Rising protectionism , trade disputes , and challenges to multilateral institutions have contributed to a more uncertain global environment . Tensions surrounding global trade governance , including the functioning of the World Trade Organization 's dispute settlement system , have raised questions about the effectiveness of existing mechanisms for resolving economic conflicts . <p> For African countries , which often rely on predictable trade rules and external markets , such developments may increase exposure to external shocks and reduce the effectiveness of traditional dispute resolution channels . In a more fragmented system , economic and political leverage may play a larger role in shaping outcomes . <p> At the same time , global military expenditure has risen significantly over the past two decades , reflecting broader geopolitical tensions . In Africa , security challenges -- including political instability , military interventions , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , particularly in the Sahel . These dynamics suggest that security risks are becoming more structural rather than episodic . <h> Great Power Rivalry and Strategic Competition <p> The intensification of strategic competition among major powers is another defining feature of the current geopolitical environment . Relations between the United States , China , and Russia have become increasingly complex , spanning trade , technology , finance , and security domains . <p> For Africa , this presents both risks and opportunities . On one hand , heightened competition may lead to increased investment , infrastructure development , and diplomatic engagement from multiple global partners . On the other hand , it may also create pressure for African countries to navigate competing interests and alignments . <p> China remains Africa 's largest trading partner and a major source of infrastructure financing , while Western countries continue to play a significant role in investment , aid , and security cooperation . Russia has also expanded its presence in certain security contexts . As these relationships evolve , African governments may face more complex strategic choices . <p> Diverging global political and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ governance , development models , and international partnerships increasingly differ across regions . In this context , African countries are likely to continue pursuing diversified partnerships , balancing relationships to maximize economic and strategic benefits . <h> Rising Risks in Global Financial Markets <p> Global financial conditions are becoming more challenging , with rising public debt levels and tighter monetary conditions in advanced economies . According to projections , global debt levels are expected to remain elevated , raising concerns about long-term fiscal sustainability in several major economies . <p> Higher interest rates in advanced markets have implications for emerging and frontier economies , including those in Africa . Borrowing costs have increased , and access to international capital markets has become more constrained for some countries . Several African economies already face relatively high debt levels , which may limit fiscal space and increase vulnerability to external shocks . <p> Currency dynamics also play an important role . Movements in the US dollar , global interest rates , and commodity prices can significantly affect African economies , particularly those reliant on imports or commodity exports . While exchange rate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ competitiveness and import costs -- the overall environment points to increased volatility . <p> These financial pressures may require policymakers to adopt more cautious fiscal and monetary strategies , while also strengthening domestic revenue systems and financial resilience . <h> Demographic Pressures and Social Stability <p> Africa 's demographic trajectory is one of its most defining characteristics . With a population exceeding 1.5 billion and a median age significantly lower than in most other regions , the continent has substantial long-term growth potential . <p> However , this demographic expansion also presents challenges . A large and rapidly growing youth population requires sustained job creation , investment in education , and expansion of economic opportunities . While youth unemployment rates vary across countries , underemployment and informal work remain widespread . <p> In some contexts , limited economic opportunities may contribute to social tensions , migration pressures , or vulnerability to recruitment by non-state armed groups . Security challenges linked to extremist organizations remain significant in certain regions , particularly where governance and economic conditions are fragile . <p> At the same time , recent years have seen an increase @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . These developments highlight both the risks and the potential associated with demographic change . With appropriate policy responses , Africa 's young population could become a major driver of economic growth and innovation . <h> Climate Risk , Food Security , and Displacement <p> Climate change represents a critical and long-term risk for African economies . Although the continent contributes a relatively small share of global emissions , it is disproportionately exposed to climate-related impacts . <p> Rising temperatures and increasing frequency of extreme weather events -- including droughts , floods , and cyclones -- are already affecting multiple regions . These changes have significant implications for agriculture , which remains a key source of employment and livelihoods across the continent . <p> Climate-related disruptions can affect food security , water availability , and rural incomes , potentially contributing to internal displacement and cross-border migration . Estimates suggest that tens of millions of people in Africa could be affected by climate-related migration in the coming decades . <p> Addressing these risks will require substantial investment in climate adaptation , resilient infrastructure , and sustainable agriculture . Strengthening early warning @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ effective responses . <h> Conclusion <p> African economies are entering a period of increased global uncertainty , shaped by geopolitical fragmentation , financial pressures , demographic shifts , and climate risks . While these challenges are significant , they also coincide with opportunities for strategic positioning , economic diversification , and institutional development . <p> To navigate this evolving landscape , African countries will need to strengthen economic resilience , invest in human capital , and pursue balanced international partnerships . Regional integration initiatives and domestic reforms will play a key role in enhancing long-term stability and growth . <p> Ultimately , the extent to which these risks translate into constraints -- or opportunities -- will depend on policy choices , governance , and the ability of African economies to adapt to a rapidly changing global environment . <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider . @@136725403 <h> IATA urges Africa to prioritise aviation for growth <p> The International Air Transport Association ( IATA ) called on African governments to prioritise aviation as a strategic enabler of economic and social development . <p> " Aviation is economic infrastructure for Africa . Its value lies in the long-term benefits it delivers . An aviation strategy focused on safety , cost-competitiveness , energy security/sustainability , and ease of doing business will create jobs , enable trade , support tourism , and further regional integration . The prosperity this generates will allow governments to push forward social and economic development more durably than any tax that might be collected from travelers , " said Kamil Alawadhi , IATA 's Regional Vice President for Africa and the Middle East . <p> A Strategy for Aviation in Africa <p> At its Focus Africa Conference in Addis Ababa , Ethiopia , IATA urged governments to pursue a comprehensive aviation strategy with the following elements : <p> 1 . Improving Safety <p> Africa has made significant progress in aviation safety . Between 2024 and 2025 , the accident rate fell from 12.13 to 7.86 @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ global average of 1.32 and is the highest among all regions . <p> To further improve safety in Africa , IATA called for all parties in IATA 's Collaborative Aviation Safety Improvement Programme ( CASIP ) to mobilise resources in three areas : <p> Increase the implementation of ICAO Standards and Recommended Practices ( SARPS ) . Average effective implementation across 46 of 48 Sub Saharan African states stands at 60.34% , compared with the global average of 69.46% and the global target of 75% . <p> Publish accident reports . Between 2019-2023 , only 19% of accident reports were completed versus a global average of 63% . Accident investigation reports that are delayed , incomplete , or unpublished withhold valuable safety insights that can improve safety . This underscores the need for improved compliance with state investigation obligations under Annex 13 of the Chicago Convention . <p> The cost of doing aviation business in Africa is high . A key element of this are the taxes and charges by governments and infrastructure providers , the burden of which is about 15% higher in Africa than the global average . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the ECOWAS December 2025 decision to eliminate aviation taxes and reduce select charges by 25% . Full and consistent implementation at the national level without further delay is critical to maximise the benefits from lowering aviation costs . <p> Preserving residence-based corporate taxation of airlines . Proposals emerging from African countries in UN tax discussions on source-based taxation should be rejected . The cross-border nature of aviation makes residence-based ( tax paid at the headquarters location ) the most efficient and fair method for corporate taxation . Source-based taxation would risk double taxation ( or worse ) as the ' source ' for any one ticket is often spread across multiple jurisdictions . <p> 3 . Ease of Doing Business <p> Removing roadblocks to ease doing business is essential for aviation to thrive . IATA highlighted two areas of particular concern : <p> Ensure frictionless repatriation of revenues in line with global standards . While treaties and bilateral agreements stipulate the right of airlines to repatriate revenues earned across their networks , governments ' failure to comply with these obligations results in funds being blocked . African countries account for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ total of $774 million blocked as of end-March 2026 . <p> " Given the scale of funds blocked in Algeria , urgent and decisive government action in Algeria is essential . But our efforts to engage with the Ministry of Trade and Export Promotion and the Central Bank have been met with little responsiveness and airlines continue to face delays despite complying with burdensome requirements . In Algeria , and all locations where airlines are denied access to their revenues , governments must engage with the industry to find a sustainable solution or risk the consequences on connectivity , " said Alawadhi . <p> Recent disruptions to the global energy supply have highlighted the link between energy security and sustainability , particularly the production of Sustainable Aviation Fuel ( SAF ) . IATA noted the significant benefits that Africa can gain in energy security , jobs , and revenue from aligning its efforts on sustainability to the global approach : <p> Support CORSIA and make Eligible Emission Units ( EEUs ) available . CORSIA is the only globally agreed economic measure to manage aviation 's climate change impact . The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ available to airlines who need them to fulfil their CORSIA obligations . While this could be a significant source of climate finance for the continent , only Tanzania , Malawi , Rwanda , Gambia , Sierra Leone , Madagascar , and Nigeria have taken initial steps to enter the market . IATA urges all African governments to make use of their potential in line with the provisions of the Paris Agreement . <p> Promote SAF production . IATA 's Global Feedstock Assessment shows that Sub-Saharan Africa could supply up to 106 million tonnes of SAF-suitable feedstock by 2050 , largely from agricultural residues , forestry waste , and municipal solid waste . This could be supplemented with energy crops grown on marginal or degraded land areas . With strong , predictable incentive-based policies and investments in collections and processing infrastructure , the current 1.5 ? Mt of announced renewable fuel capacity could grow exponentially , creating jobs and shoring up energy security . <p> Disclaimer : The content of this article is syndicated or provided to this website from an external third party provider . It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald . <p> When King Charles III stood before the US Congress this week , he did something that British politicians increasingly struggle to do : he spoke , and people listened . Not because he holds power , but because he does n't . <p> That is the paradox at the centre of Britain 's foreign policy right now . As relations between the United Kingdom and United States strain over the ongoing conflict in Iran -- with Keir Starmer refusing to join military action -- Britain has reached for one of its oldest tools : the monarchy . <p> That is what soft power looks like in practice . <p> The term ' soft power , ' coined by Joseph Nye , describes the ability of a state to influence without coercion -- to shape outcomes not through force , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is often misunderstood as something vague or ornamental . Cultural exports . Nice speeches . Diplomatic niceties . But that misses the point . Soft power is not what is said . It is about what becomes possible because of what was said . <p> ( Image : PA ) <p> In his address , the King did not negotiate policy . He could not . As a constitutional monarch , he does not set foreign policy , nor can he openly contradict the government he represents . But within those constraints , the speech was carefully constructed . He involved the Magna Carta -- not as a historical decoration , but as a reminder that even sovereign power is subject to law . He spoke of Ukraine , signalling continued British support at a time when American commitment is uncertain . He reminded everyone of Britain 's involvement in Afghanistan . He referenced climate change , a pointed contrast to the priorities of Trump . <p> None of this was accidental . This is diplomacy operating indirectly -- raising issues without confrontation , reinforcing norms without demanding compliance . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . Did the visit change American policy ? Almost certainly not . Trump is not a president known for being quietly steered by constitutional symbolism or environmental appeals . <p> But that is the wrong metric . Soft power is not about immediate concessions . It is about shaping the environment in which decisions are made . And here , the monarchy has a distinct advantage . <p> The United States has always had a complicated relationship with the monarchy . It defines itself in opposition to it -- a republic founded on the rejection of kings . And yet , it remains deeply fascinated by the institution . <p> That fascination matters . Where British politicians are treated as negotiators -- partisan , transactional , often disposable -- the monarchy is received differently . As something older , more stable , and , crucially , above the immediate fray of politics . <p> That perception gives access . It creates a space in which messages can be delivered without triggering the defensive instincts that formal diplomacy often provokes . In that sense , the King 's visit , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ independence from Britain , was not about persuading Trump directly . But it happens to come at a convenient time , when Starmer is no longer seen by the Trump administration as a fellow upholder of the alliance between the US and UK . It was about reinforcing a broader narrative : that the UK remains a partner grounded in law , continuity , and shared history -- even when it diverges on immediate strategy . <p> But this raises a more uncomfortable question . What did Britain actually gain ? Because soft power , if it is to be taken seriously , must ultimately be judged by outcomes . And here , the answer is less clear . <p> ( Image : PA ) <p> The UK did not secure a change in US policy on Iran . It did not shift the trajectory of the conflict . It did not extract concessions . What it did was maintain the relationship and try to remind the US of its values . <p> At a moment of disagreement , Britain avoided escalation . It signalled independence without rupture . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other words , it bought time . <p> There is , however , a limit to this approach . Soft power works best in a world where relationships still matter , where norms still carry weight , and where influence can be exercised directly . That world is becoming less stable . As global politics shifts towards more overt uses of power -- military , economic , coercive -- the ability to charm , persuade , or symbolically remind becomes less decisive . The monarchy can open doors . It can not force outcomes . <p> But after Trump 's ramblings on his social media about Starmer 's weakness and growing indifference to the alliance , soft power in the form of a state visit seems to be the last straw to pull in order to ease tensions . <p> And so Britain continues to rely on it . @@136759803 <p> The recent pastoralist -- farmer tensions reported in Kitui County , Kenya , are a powerful reminder that climate security is no longer an abstract policy debate . <p> As drought conditions intensify in traditionally arid areas , herders are being forced to move farther in search of pasture and water , creating new migratory routes across counties once outside seasonal grazing patterns . <p> In Kitui , the movement of livestock into farming zones has heightened tensions over crops , land use and access to scarce resources . It is a local story with a regional meaning : climate change is reshaping mobility , livelihoods and security across the Horn of Africa . <p> The Horn of Africa remains one of the world 's most climate-vulnerable regions , battered by droughts , floods and heatwaves . <p> These extreme weather events are no longer isolated environmental shocks ; they are part of a growing climate -- conflict -- migration nexus threatening the security , livelihoods and stability of millions . It is a daily reality disrupting economies , straining governance institutions and unsettling social systems . <p> Over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for repeated climate shocks . Severe flooding struck during the March -- May rainy seasons of 2018 , 2020 and 2024 , as well as later seasonal rains in 2019 , 2023 and 2024 . <p> These floods often followed prolonged droughts , including the devastating 2020 -- 2023 drought -- the worst in 70 years . <p> Across the Intergovernmental Authority on Development ( Igad ) region , the drought caused the loss of more than 13 million livestock . In Kenya alone , the government estimated the economic cost of livestock loss at more than $1.5 billion . <p> Human tollThe humanitarian toll is staggering . The region finds itself caught in a convergence of crises , where conflict collides with climate shocks while economic fragility feeds political instability -- a vicious cycle in which , when one system fails , others inevitably follow . <p> In 2025 , an estimated 42 million people across six Igad member states -- Djibouti , Eritrea , Ethiopia , Kenya , Somalia , South Sudan , Sudan , and Uganda -- faced high levels of acute food insecurity , while over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> The scale of the crisis reflects a long-term deterioration : in five countries with comparable data since 2016 -- Kenya , Somalia , South Sudan , Sudan and Uganda -- the number of people in crisis or worse ( IPC Phase 3 or above ) has tripled , from 13.9 million in 2016 to 41.7 million in 2025 . <p> Not only has climate change worsened food security in the region , it has also severely affected human mobility . <p> In 2023 , across the Horn of Africa , at least 31.9 million people were in urgent need of life-saving and life-sustaining assistance due to the most prolonged and severe drought in recent history . <p> Families took desperate measures to survive , with more than 2.7 million people leaving their homes due to drought in search of food , pasture , water and alternative livelihoods , increasing the risk of inter-communal conflict , as well as heightening pressure on already limited basic services . <p> In the years after the drought , disaster displacement across the Horn of Africa remains severe , driven by the compounding @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 314,000 flood displacements in 2024 , while insufficient rains left nearly 757,000 people displaced in Ethiopia and over 733,000 in Somalia at year 's end -- unable to return home after years of drought . <p> South Sudan recorded 423,000 flood displacements in 2024 , frequently forcing people already uprooted by conflict to flee again . <p> Conflict link <p> These numbers illustrate the drivers of the climate security nexus . @@136760881 <p> Along with wind , rain and lightning , the weather may bring about unexpected health problems . Acute attacks of " thunderstorm asthma " can worsen pollen allergies and exacerbate respiratory conditions . And as climate change is likely to cause more storms in the future , more people will be put at risk . <h> Storm surge <p> Generally , " rain tends to lower pollen counts by cleansing the air , and many people find that rainy weather tends to reduce asthma symptoms triggered by allergies , " said Harvard Health Publishing . But thunderstorms are an exception because they can cause cold downdrafts , which " concentrate air particles , such as pollen and mold . " The particles are then " swept up into clouds where humidity is high , " and " wind , humidity and lightning break up the particles to a size that can readily enter the nose , sinuses and lungs . " Strong gusts of wind disperse the pollen and mold , irritating lungs . <p> The rapid breakdown and spread of air particles can cause thunderstorm asthma . " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , " Clifford Bassett , the founder and medical director at Allergy and Asthma Care of New York , said to The Weather Channel . The phenomenon is caused by a " complex interaction between environmental and meteorological factors , coupled with intense aeroallergen exposure in susceptible individuals , " Constance H. Katelaris , a senior staff specialist of immunology and allergy at Campbelltown Hospital and Western Sydney University , said at InSight+ . <p> Those most likely to experience thunderstorm asthma are people with pollen allergies and hay fever ( rhinitis ) , as well as those with preexisting asthma and poor asthma control . Adults in their third or fourth decade of life appear to be especially susceptible . Older children are also vulnerable , being in the " peak ages for expression of allergic rhinitis , " said Katelaris . There may also be a " significantly increased risk among individuals of Asian and Indian descent , " according to data from the " largest and deadliest episode of thunderstorm asthma recorded to date , " in Melbourne in 2016 . " Six of the 10 people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <h> A big storm 's a-coming <p> While thunderstorm asthma " may seem like more of a curiosity than a serious threat to public health , " when it " affects a large population area , emergency rooms can become overwhelmed , " said Harvard Health Publishing . During the Melbourne episode , over 3,400 people experienced severe asthma symptoms and 10 people died . " Any pollen , any dust , anything that is sitting on the ground will be dispersed , and it will be blown onto cars , into the circulating air , perhaps into homes , if the windows are open , and onto anyone who is outside and unfortunate to be in the path , " meteorologist Dante Ricci said to National Geographic . <p> Cases of thunderstorm asthma are expected to increase in the future due to climate change . Globally warming temperatures can lead to " prolonged allergenic pollen seasons combined with increased pollen allergenicity , as well as heightened likelihood of extreme weather events , " said a review published in The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology : In Practice . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ have asthma and about 81 million people have seasonal allergies , " said Harvard Health Publishing .
